verdict.rationale: The proposition narrows the wider ministry question to visible leading acts done before the gathered mixed assembly, and a direct query of the lexical store confirms that the load-bearing vocabulary pulls in two directions on exactly that point. Female audible participation is positively assumed: 1Cor.11.5 reads pasa de gyne proseuchomene e propheteuousa, every woman praying or prophesying, with two present participles nominative singular feminine; the verb propheteuo (G4395) occurs 28 times across the canon and is applied directly to four daughters of Philip propheteuousai in Acts.21.9, to daughters and handmaidens in Acts.2.17-18, to Anna prophetis (G4398) in Luke.2.36, and to a woman prophetis at Thyatira in Rev.2.20. Phoebe is named diakonos (G1249, 30 occurrences) of the assembly at Cenchreae in Rom.16.1 and prostatis (G4368) of many in Rom.16.2, where prostatis is a hapax occurring nowhere else in the canon. Priscilla, named before Aquila in the verified Acts.18.26 token order, joins in ektithemi (G1620, the same verb of doctrinal exposition used of Paul in Acts.28.23) setting out the way of God to Apollos in a private taking-aside. Against a broad public platform stand 1Cor.14.34, where the verb is the general sigao (G4601, 9 occurrences including 1Cor.14.28 and 1Cor.14.30 where each is bounded by an ean conditional governing a specific disorder) and the still more general lalein, and 1Tim.2.12 where didaskein is coupled with the hapax authentein (G0831 occurs once only in the entire New Testament). Because the silence verb is the same lexeme used two other times in the same chapter inside situation-bound conditionals and because the second restriction verb is a one-occurrence hapax whose sense cannot be triangulated, the line between an audibly assumed prophecy or prayer and an absolutely silenced speaking is not fixed by morphology, and the cited words name no category corresponding to leading congregational singing, leading public prayer, reading Scripture aloud, sharing testimony, or making announcements. The lexical pattern is materially contested rather than decisive.

scripture.force: pasa de gyne proseuchomene e propheteuousa akatakalypto te kephale, every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered. The two present participles proseuchomene, praying, and propheteuousa, prophesying, are nominative singular feminine and presuppose the act as actually occurring; the verse regulates only the manner, an uncovered head dishonors her head, and issues no prohibition. The parallel 1Cor.11.4 uses the identical participles in the masculine for a man, so the grammar treats male and female praying and prophesying as the same kind of act to be ordered, not forbidden. The lexemes do not state the setting and do not classify praying and prophesying as a non-teaching platform-leading act as distinct from the authoritative function restricted elsewhere, so the passage supports female vocal participation in general without deciding whether leading congregational singing, public prayer, or Scripture reading before the mixed assembly is in view.

toutoi de esan thygateres tessares parthenoi propheteuousai, this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied. The present participle propheteuousai is nominative plural feminine, agreeing directly with the four daughters, and the narrative reports actual ongoing female prophetic ministry as an unremarkable feature of church life. A concordance query confirms the same lemma propheteuo occurs 28 times across the canon including at Acts.2.17-18 of daughters and handmaidens and at Rev.11.3 of the two witnesses, so the act of prophesying is a pan-canonical category not bounded by gender. The narrative gives no setting, audience, or relation to the gathered mixed assembly, so it supports audible female ministry without by itself deciding whether such speech is a leading role in the worship gathering or a charismatic gift exercised elsewhere.

Anna is called prophetis, prophetess, a feminine noun whose only other canonical occurrence is at Rev.2.20 in a negative use of a woman at Thyatira. The narrative continues that Anna did not depart from the temple and elalei concerning the child to all looking for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke.2.38), so the lexeme combined with the imperfect of laleo attributes recognized prophetic standing and audible public proclamation in a worship setting to a named woman, anchoring a public female prophetic ministry pattern in the Gospel narrative. The text does not name a defined platform-leading category, so it complicates a strict ban without by itself fixing the scope of the proposition.

synistemi de hymin Phoiben ten adelphen hemon, ousan kai diakonon tes ekklesias tes en Kenchreais, I commend to you Phoebe our sister, being also a diakonos of the assembly at Cenchreae. The noun diakonos, here in the accusative feminine attached to a named woman in connection with a local ekklesia, is the same lexeme used for recognized service roles elsewhere; a concordance query shows 30 canon occurrences including 1Tim.3.8,12 of office-holders, Col.1.7 of Epaphras, and Rom.13.4 of the civil minister, so the word ranges from general service to designated office without by itself fixing the activity. The phrase tes ekklesias attaches her standing explicitly to the local assembly, which supports a recognized public role for a woman, but diakonos alone does not specify whether her role included any leading act in the gathered meeting.

kai gar aute prostatis pollon egenethe kai emou autou, for she has been a prostatis of many and of me myself. A concordance query confirms prostatis (G4368) is a hapax occurring only here in the entire canon, so its precise force cannot be triangulated from any parallel use. The cognate verb proistemi means to stand before or to lead, and the masculine prostates in extra-canonical Greek covers patron, protector, leader, and chief. The applied sense to Phoebe is therefore lexically thin: it ranges between patron-benefactor and one who stands before others in leadership, and Paul applying it to himself as object, emou autou, places her in a posture of active support that has standing-before-others as part of its semantic range. The lexeme leans toward female leadership in some sense but does not name a worship-gathering leading act and does not by itself settle whether a woman led the mixed assembly in singing, prayer, or reading.

aspasasthe Andronikon kai Iounian tous syngeneis mou, greet Andronicus and Junia my kinsfolk, hoitines eisin episemoi en tois apostolois. A concordance query confirms Iounia (G2458) occurs once only in the canon at this verse, so the form is a hapax. The accented form distinguishes the feminine Junia from a contracted masculine Junias, and the manuscript and accentual evidence is itself a known crux that the bundle does not resolve from the lexicon alone. The phrase episemoi en tois apostolois is grammatically ambiguous between inclusive, noteworthy among the apostles, and exclusive, well known to the apostles. The verse therefore complicates the proposition either by naming a woman within the apostolic circle or by leaving the question open at two distinct levels, the sex of the person and the syntactic scope of episemoi.

proselabonto auton kai akribesteron auto exethento ten hodon tou theou, they took him aside and set out the way of God to him more accurately. A direct token-order query of the lexical store confirms Priscilla (G4252) is named before Aquila (G0207) in this witness. The verb ektithemi (G1620, only 4 canon occurrences including Acts.28.23 of Paul expounding the kingdom of God) is here aorist middle third plural, attributing serious doctrinal exposition jointly to husband and wife, and akribesteron, more accurately, marks the content as doctrinal correction. The narrative supports active female word ministry toward a man, but proselabonto, took aside, marks a private setting rather than the gathered mixed assembly, so it does not establish a public platform-leading role and complicates rather than decides the assembly question.

hai gynaikes en tais ekklesiais sigatosan, ou gar epitrepetai autais lalein, the women are to keep silent in the assemblies, for it is not permitted them to speak. A direct query confirms the verb sigao (G4601) occurs 9 times across the canon, including the same chapter at 1Cor.14.28 where a tongue-speaker is to sigato if there is no interpreter and at 1Cor.14.30 where a prophet is to sigato when another receives a revelation, each inside an ean conditional governing a specific disorder. The prohibited activity is named with the general lalein, to speak, not a verb specific to authoritative teaching, and the location en tais ekklesiais bears directly on whether leading singing, public prayer, or Scripture reading before the mixed assembly is permitted. Because three uses of sigao in this single chapter are situation-bound and the speech-verb is general, the scope between absolute silence and a regulation of disruptive speech is not fixed by the morphology, which is the crux of the dispute.

ei de ti mathein thelousin, en oiko tous idious andras eperotatosan, aischron gar estin gynaiki lalein en ekklesia, if they wish to learn anything let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the assembly. The conditional ties the silenced lalein to wanting to learn and to asking questions, which on one reading frames the silenced speech as disorderly in-assembly questioning rather than as prophecy or prayer. On the alternative reading the explanatory gar generalizes the prohibition to any female lalein in the assembly, and the noun aischron, shameful, attaches a categorical valuation. The lexemes do not rank these two readings, so the scope of the immediately prior silence command remains contested by the morphology of this clause as well.

didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepo oude authentein andros, all einai en hesychia, I do not permit a woman to teach or to authentein over a man, but to be in quietness. A concordance query confirms authenteo (G0831) is a hapax occurring once only in the entire New Testament, here, so its sense between to exercise ordinary authority and to domineer or usurp cannot be triangulated from parallel canonical usage. The two present infinitives didaskein and authentein are joined by oude, which may name two distinct prohibited acts or one composite idea, to teach in a domineering manner. The noun hesychia (G2271) occurs 4 times, including 2Thess.3.12 of working quietly with a settled manner of life and Acts.22.2 of a crowd growing quiet to listen, so en hesychia describes demeanor rather than absolute muteness. The text restricts a teaching-with-authority act over a man but does not name leading congregational singing, public prayer, or Scripture reading, so it neither clearly includes nor clearly excludes the practice in question.

complicating_texts.resolution: A direct token-order query confirms Priscilla is named before Aquila in this witness, and the plural verb exethento, from ektithemi, governs the doctrinal object the way of God with Apollos as the one instructed. The same verb describes Paul expounding the kingdom in Acts.28.23, so it denotes serious doctrinal exposition. It is addressed by noting that the verb proselabonto marks a private taking-aside rather than the public assembly, so the narrative shows joint female doctrinal instruction of a man without establishing a public platform-leading act before the gathered assembly. The text genuinely supports broad female ministry yet leaves the specific assembly-leading question open, which is why it complicates rather than resolves the verdict.

A morphology query gives proseuchomene and propheteuousa as present participles nominative singular feminine attached to gyne, so the verse assumes audible female prayer and prophecy in the gathering and regulates only the manner of head covering. It is addressed by observing that the lexemes do not state the setting and do not classify praying or prophesying as a non-teaching platform-leading act as opposed to the authoritative function restricted elsewhere, so the passage supports female vocal participation without deciding whether leading congregational singing, public prayer, or Scripture reading before the mixed assembly is included. The relation between this assumed speech and the silence command of 1Cor.14.34 is itself part of the contested matter.

A concordance query confirms prostatis (G4368) is a hapax occurring only here in the entire canon, so its sense between female patron-benefactor and one who stands before others in leadership cannot be triangulated from any parallel use. It is addressed by noting that the cognate stem proistemi means to stand before or to lead, while attested Hellenistic usage of the related masculine carries patron, protector, leader; the applied force to Phoebe therefore ranges across this band without naming a worship-gathering leading act. The text contributes to the openness side without resolving the specific platform-leadership question.

A concordance query confirms Iounia (G2458) occurs once only in the canon at this verse, so it is a hapax. The grammatical gender of the form, between feminine Iounia and contracted masculine Iounias, depends on accentuation that the bundled lexical layer alone cannot fully fix, and the phrase episemoi en tois apostolois is grammatically ambiguous between inclusive, noteworthy among the apostles, and exclusive, well known to the apostles. Because both the referent's sex and the syntactic scope are contested at the level of the words themselves, the verse pulls in opposite directions depending on resolution of two underdetermined lexical points that the available data cannot settle, so the matter is left unresolved and flagged.

The silence command is widely held to carry a transposition in part of the manuscript tradition, where some Western witnesses place verses 34 and 35 after verse 40, and some have argued the unit is a later interpolation, which bears on how absolutely the command should be read. A direct query of the lexical store confirms the ingested variant units cover the 3 John window only, the targeted search for any variant unit in 1 Corinthians 14 returns nothing, and not_in_ecm_scope is true for these anchors, so the placement and originality question cannot be examined on the available data. Because the location and the absolute-versus-situational scope of this command bear directly on the proposition and cannot be resolved here, the matter is left unresolved and flagged, and it is part of why the verdict is recorded as variant-sensitive.

variants.note: A direct query of the lexical store confirms the ingested variant units are scoped to 3 John only, the targeted search for any variant unit in 1 Corinthians 14 returned zero results, and not_in_ecm_scope is true for the cited anchors. The surface text of the anchor verses carries editorial sigla, marked by the symbols at autes in 1Cor.11.5, at kai in Rom.16.1, and at the bracketed phrases in Acts.18.26 and Acts.21.9, which signal contested wording in the witnesses. More importantly the closely related 1Cor.14.34-35 silence unit, which bears on whether assembly leading is permitted, is well known to carry a transposition in part of the Western tradition where the verses follow verse 40, and the originality of the unit has been contested. The accentuation of Iounia in Rom.16.7 between feminine and masculine is a related minuscule-era reading question that also bears on adjacent ministry texts. Because the placement and originality of the silence command bear directly on the practice under test, the verdict is marked variant-sensitive. These books fall outside the published CBGM scope, which covers 3 John only, so the status is recorded as ecm-shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the 1Cor.14.34 sigatosan as governing public assembly speech that carries a leading or directive function, so that visibly leading the gathered mixed assembly in singing, prayer, or Scripture reading is taken as an authoritative function reserved to men under the headship pattern of 1Cor.11.3 and the restriction of 1Tim.2.12. On this reading the praying and prophesying assumed in 1Cor.11.5, the four daughters of Acts.21.9, Anna in Luke.2.36, the diakonos and prostatis terms of Rom.16.1-2, and the joint exposition of Acts.18.26 describe gifting, service, and patronage that do not amount to leading the gathered mixed assembly in a directive capacity, since none of these passages names leading congregational singing, public prayer, or Scripture reading as a defined role. The headship logic of 1Cor.11.3 read together with the 1Tim.2.13 creation-order gar grounds the restriction trans-culturally, so the specific platform-leading practice is not clearly licensed and likely falls under restriction even though no single lexeme decides the case.

Reads the 1Cor.14.34 sigao alongside the chapter's other situational silencings at verses 28 and 30 and the general verb lalein as a regulation of disruptive speech rather than an absolute bar, with v35 framing the silenced speech as in-assembly questioning to be deferred to the home. It takes the assumed proseuchomene and propheteuousa of 1Cor.11.5, the prophesying daughters of Acts.21.9, the prophetis Anna who elalei in the temple at Luke.2.36 and Luke.2.38, and the prophetis at Thyatira in Rev.2.20 as audible assembly participation, reads diakonos and the hapax prostatis in Rom.16.1-2 as recognized service and standing-before-others leadership, the Acts.18.26 joint ektithemi with Priscilla named first as significant doctrinal teaching of a man, and the inclusive reading of episemoi en tois apostolois at Rom.16.7 as a woman within apostolic standing. The en hesychia of 1Tim.2.11-12 describes demeanor, parallel to 2Thess.3.12, and the restricting authenteo is a one-occurrence hapax of narrow disputed sense. On this reading non-teaching leading acts such as leading singing, public prayer, and Scripture reading fall within the assumed female vocal participation and outside the narrowly restricted authoritative teaching, so the practice is permitted and the broader category of authoritative ministry is itself open.

Reads the restrictive directives as a step within a trajectory whose direction, traced from the female praying, prophesying, serving, patronage, and joint exposition of 1Cor.11.5, Acts.21.9, Luke.2.36, Rom.16.1-2, Rom.16.7, and Acts.18.26, points beyond a first-century application. On this reading whether visible non-teaching leading of the mixed assembly is permitted depends on a movement the cited lexemes do not themselves resolve, since the creation-order gar of 1Tim.2.13 anchors instruction in its setting while the canonical presence of women prophesying and expounding signals movement, leaving the practice contested on the words alone.

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses operate on the same queried anchor lemmas and reach different conclusions by reading sigao and lalein in 1Cor.14.34-35 as either absolute or situational, by deciding whether the assumed praying and prophesying of 1Cor.11.5 and the prophetic standing of Luke.2.36 and Acts.21.9 count as leading acts or only as gifts, by construing diakonos and the hapax prostatis in Rom.16.1-2 as office and leadership or as service and patronage, by resolving the dual ambiguity of Iounia and episemoi en tois apostolois in Rom.16.7 inclusively or exclusively, by reading en hesychia of 1Tim.2.11-12 as demeanor or as full silence, and by drawing the boundary between a non-teaching leading function and the authoritative function restricted by the hapax authenteo in 1Tim.2.12. A reader holding any one lens should find its strongest lexical form represented here. The disagreement is over the scope of contested lexemes, the resolution of two hapax restrictions and three hapax positive cases, and the unstated category of platform leading, not over agreed morphology, which the queries confirm, so the lexical pattern is contested rather than decisive.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Determine whether the canonical lexical pattern permits or forbids women performing visible audible acts before the gathered mixed assembly such as leading congregational singing, leading public prayer, reading Scripture aloud, sharing testimony, or making announcements, examining the assumed praying and prophesying of 1Cor.11.5, the prophesying daughters of Acts.21.9, the prophetis Anna in Luke.2.36, the diakonos and prostatis of Rom.16.1-2, the possibly female apostolic standing of Rom.16.7, and the private joint exposition of Acts.18.26 alongside the assembly silence of 1Cor.14.34-35 and the teaching-with-authority restriction of 1Tim.2.12, without presupposing that a non-teaching leading category exists in the cited words or that it falls cleanly on either side of the silence command.
stem_audit.notes: The stem builds in a category, non-teaching platform-leadership, and a contrast, leading versus exercising authoritative teaching, that the cited texts do not lexically supply, since no verse names leading congregational singing, leading public prayer, reading Scripture, sharing testimony, or making announcements as a defined role. By framing these as non-teaching it presupposes that such acts can be cleanly separated from the authoritative function that the hapax authenteo and the assembly silence of 1Cor.14.34 govern, which is precisely the contested boundary. Direct queries confirm three lexical hapaxes are load-bearing here in opposite directions: prostatis (G4368) appears only at Rom.16.2, Iounia (G2458) only at Rom.16.7, and authenteo (G0831) only at 1Tim.2.12, so the verdict is structurally underdetermined by the words at three pivotal points at once. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the audit records that the lexicon furnishes neither a category of platform leading nor a settled scope for sigao, lalein, or authenteo that would place these acts inside or outside the restriction. Verdict unchanged from the prior file.

lay_summary: The question asks whether women may take visible leading roles in the mixed church gathering that are not teaching, such as leading the singing, leading the public prayer, reading the Bible aloud, sharing a testimony, or giving the announcements. The original-language words pull in two directions, which is the heart of the dispute. On one side, several texts show women audibly active in worship and ministry. First Corinthians 11:5 speaks of every woman praying or prophesying and only adjusts how she does it, with the same participles used one verse earlier for a man. Acts 21:9 records four daughters who were prophesying. Luke 2:36 calls Anna a prophetess and verse 38 says she spoke of the child to all in the temple. Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe a diakonos, a servant or minister, of her local assembly, and Romans 16:2 calls her a prostatis, a word that occurs only once in the whole New Testament and ranges from patron to one who stands before others. Acts 18:26 shows Priscilla, named before her husband in the verified copies, jointly explaining the way of God to Apollos using a strong word for doctrinal exposition, though in a private setting. Romans 16:7 greets Junia, a name that on one reading is a woman noted within the circle of the apostles, but the form occurs only once and the scope of the phrase is itself ambiguous. On the other side, First Corinthians 14:34 says the women should keep silent in the assemblies and uses a general word for speaking, set squarely in the gathered meeting, so it bears directly on whether a woman may lead audible acts there. Yet the very same silence word is used twice nearby for a tongue-speaker or a prophet who should fall silent in a particular situation, so it is not clear whether the command is absolute or aimed at a specific disorder. First Timothy 2:12 restricts a woman from teaching or from a second act named by a verb that occurs only once in the whole New Testament, so its exact force cannot be pinned down. The cited verses never name leading singing, leading prayer, or reading Scripture as a defined role. The trouble is that three of the load-bearing words are single-occurrence hapaxes pulling in opposite directions, and the silence word is the same lexeme used in clearly situation-bound contexts nearby. Because the same vocabulary supports both a more open and a more restrictive conclusion, and because the silence text carries a known manuscript question about where it belongs, the lexical pattern here is genuinely contested rather than decisive.
